starterQuestions.q: What is the standard diploid chromosome number and sex chromosome complement in a human male?
starterQuestions.a: 46,XY (46 chromosomes total: 44 autosomes and two sex chromosomes X and Y).
The failure of homologous chromosomes (meiosis I) or sister chromatids (meiosis II / mitosis) to separate correctly during anaphase.

starterQuestions.q: What proportion of gametes are abnormal if nondisjunction occurs in meiosis I versus meiosis II?
starterQuestions.a: Meiosis I nondisjunction yields 100% abnormal gametes (two n+1, two n-1); meiosis II yields 50% abnormal gametes (one n+1, one n-1, two normal n).

starterQuestions.q: State the karyotypic formula for a female with Down's syndrome resulting from complete trisomy 21.
Which sex chromosome monosomy is compatible with postnatal human survival?
Why do acrocentric chromosomes undergo Robertsonian translocations?
starterQuestions.a: Their short p-arms contain redundant ribosomal RNA tandem repeats, allowing centromeric fusion of two long q-arms without loss of vital genetic material.

courseName: OCR Level 3 Cambridge Advanced National (AAQ) in Human Biology - Unit F172: Genetics
focus: Cytogenetics, Meiotic Nondisjunction & Karyotypic Aneuploidy Syndromes
deliverable: Diagram homologous vs sister chromatid nondisjunction during meiosis I and II, interpret diagnostic G-band karyotypes and FISH signals, and compare autosomal trisomies with sex chromosome aneuploidies.

objectives.knowledge: Explain the cytogenetic mechanisms of numerical (aneuploidy) and structural chromosomal abnormalities.
objectives.application: Differentiate the gametic consequences of nondisjunction in meiosis I versus meiosis II.
objectives.evaluation: Evaluate diagnostic cytogenetic tools (karyotyping, FISH, aCGH, NIPT) and correlate karyotypes with clinical phenotypes.

terminology.def: An abnormal chromosome number involving loss or gain of individual chromosomes (e.g. 2n+1 trisomy, 2n-1 monosomy).
Failure of paired chromosomes or sister chromatids to disjoin during meiotic anaphase, producing aneuploid gametes.
Non-reciprocal translocation fusing the long q-arms of two acrocentric chromosomes (13, 14, 15, 21, 22) at their centromeres.
Molecular cytogenetic technique using fluorescently labelled DNA probes to detect specific chromosomal sequences on metaphase spreads or interphase nuclei.

theoryPoints: Maternal Age Effect: Human oocytes enter meiotic arrest in prophase I (dictyotene) before birth; prolonged arrest over decades degrades cohesin rings, escalating nondisjunction risk.

Autosomal vs Sex Chromosome Tolerance: Autosomal monosomies are embryonic lethal. Autosomal trisomies (21, 18, 13) survive only for gene-poor chromosomes. Sex chromosome aneuploidies (45,X, 47,XXY) are well-tolerated due to X-inactivation (Barr bodies) and low Y gene content.
Down's Syndrome Cytogenetic Origins: ~95% maternal meiotic nondisjunction, ~4% Robertsonian translocation (e.g. rob(14;21)), and ~1% post-zygotic mitotic mosaicism.

Down's & Alzheimer's Link: The Amyloid Precursor Protein (APP) gene is located on chromosome 21q21.3; trisomy 21 produces lifelong 1.5-fold APP gene dosage, causing neuropathological amyloid plaque deposition by age 40.

workedExample.title: Meiotic Nondisjunction Gamete Analysis
workedExample.subtitle: Tracking chromosome 21 segregation across Meiosis I vs Meiosis II failure

steps.label: Step 1: Normal Meiosis
steps.detail: Meiosis I separates maternal and paternal homologues (2 x 1n); Meiosis II separates sister chromatids. Result: 4 normal haploid gametes (n = 23).

steps.label: Step 2: Meiosis I Nondisjunction
steps.detail: Homologues fail to separate at Anaphase I. Secondary spermatocytes/oocytes receive 24 and 22 chromosomes. Result: Two disomic (n+1) and two nullisomic (n-1) gametes (100% abnormal).

steps.label: Step 3: Fertilization by Normal Gamete
steps.detail: Fertilization by normal 23-chromosome sperm: Disomic gametes produce Trisomy 21 (47,XX/XY,+21); Nullisomic gametes produce Monosomy 21 (45,XX/XY,-21; embryonic lethal).

steps.label: Step 4: Meiosis II Contrast
steps.detail: Normal Meiosis I, followed by sister chromatid nondisjunction in one cell during Anaphase II. Result: One disomic (n+1), one nullisomic (n-1), and two normal haploid (n) gametes (50% abnormal).

hingeQuestions.question: If meiotic nondisjunction of chromosome 21 occurs during Meiosis I of oogenesis, what will be the chromosomal constitution of the resulting four gametes?
options: Two normal haploid (n) gametes, one disomic (n+1), and one nullisomic (n-1)
Two disomic (n+1) gametes and two nullisomic (n-1) gametes (100% abnormal)
hingeQuestions.explanation: Meiosis I nondisjunction leaves one daughter cell with both homologous chromosomes and the other with none, yielding 100% abnormal gametes upon completion of meiosis.

hingeQuestions.question: Why is complete monosomy of an autosome (such as Monosomy 21) universally lethal in early human embryonic development, whereas Monosomy X (Turner's syndrome: 45,X) is viable?
options: Autosomes do not contain essential genes
Autosomal monosomy unmasks lethal recessive mutations and creates catastrophic haploinsufficiency across hundreds of genes; normal females inactivate one X chromosome anyway (Lyonisation)
The X chromosome contains no functional genes
Sperm cells provide extra autosomes during fertilization
hingeQuestions.explanation: Autosomal monosomies cause severe haploinsufficiency and unmask lethal recessive alleles. Sex chromosomes are regulated by X-inactivation (Barr bodies), making X chromosome dosage abnormalities far more viable.

hingeQuestions.question: A newborn infant presents with micrognathia, low-set malformed ears, clenched fists with overlapping index fingers, and rocker-bottom feet. Which cytogenetic condition is most strongly suspected?
hingeQuestions.explanation: Overlapping fingers (index over middle), micrognathia, rocker-bottom feet, and severe cardiac defects are pathognomonic clinical features of Trisomy 18 (Edwards syndrome).

examQuestion.question: Explain the molecular mechanisms that cause Down's syndrome, distinguishing between standard meiotic nondisjunction and Robertsonian translocations, and evaluate the diagnostic advantages of Non-Invasive Prenatal Testing (NIPT) over amniocentesis. [6 marks]
guidance: Meiotic Nondisjunction: 95% of cases arise from maternal nondisjunction (cohesin breakdown in prolonged prophase I arrest), producing an extra free chromosome 21 (47,XX/XY,+21) [2 marks].

Robertsonian Translocation: ~4% of cases involve fusion of acrocentric chromosome 21q to another acrocentric (typically 14q); balanced carrier parents face high recurrence risk because translocation is heritable [2 marks].

NIPT vs Amniocentesis: Amniocentesis is invasive (needle insertion, ~0.5% miscarriage risk) though definitive; NIPT analyses cell-free fetal DNA (cfDNA) in maternal blood from 10 weeks gestation with >99% sensitivity for trisomy 21 and zero procedural miscarriage risk [2 marks].

plenary: Chromosomal abnormalities reflect large-scale disruptions involving hundreds to thousands of genes simultaneously.
Understanding nondisjunction mechanisms and cytogenetic karyotyping provides essential clinical grounding for prenatal diagnosis and genetic counselling.
Next Lesson: Genetic disorders: Polygenic and complex traits — GWAS architecture, polygenic risk scores (PRS), and multifactorial disease.
